tagline.text: Two hours from Manila, a forest waterfall pouring into a jade-colored pool

image.credit: Elmer B. Domingo / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A waterfall in Tanay, the tourism capital of Rizal province, where water spills in several streams down a moss-covered rock wall into an emerald pool. Close to town with a short walk in, it's a family-friendly day-trip spot near Manila where kids and grandparents can enjoy the water together.
Daranak Falls sits in Tanay, Rizal province, about
55km

east of Manila. Tanay lies between the southern foothills of the Sierra Madre and Laguna Lake, and with Mount Daraitan, waterfalls, and scenic mountain roads all clustered here, it's known as "Rizal's tourism capital." Daranak Falls is the longest-loved swimming spot among them.
The falls are about

high — not especially tall — but the way the water splits into several streams down a wide rock wall makes for a beautiful sight. The rock is thickly covered in green moss, and the pool below turns turquoise and emerald in the sunlight. The name is said to come from "dadanak," Tagalog for "to flow."

As a resort managed by Tanay municipality, a paved walkway and steps lead from the entrance to the falls, and there are changing rooms, restrooms, and shaded huts. The falls are just a few minutes' walk from the parking lot, so there's no real hiking involved, and the cold, clear water is perfect for cooling off on a hot day.

It suits families who want relaxed swimming rather than adventure, and travelers bringing kids to see a Philippine waterfall for the first time. Pair it with nearby Batlag Falls, the Spanish-era Tanay Church, Regina Rica with its giant Marian statue on a hill, and the view cafes along the mountain road Marcos Highway for a full day trip.
Swim in the wide pool below the falls. The edges are shallow but it deepens toward the falls, so if you're not a confident swimmer, rent a life vest at the entrance.

blocks.title: Photos in front of the falls

children.text: The moss-covered rock wall and turquoise water make for great photos. Go right after opening when there are fewer people, when the water is clearest and you can shoot without crowds.
Renting a shaded hut and table around the pool to eat a packed lunch is the classic Filipino way to visit a waterfall. With plenty of families around, weekends have a lively atmosphere.
A waterfall in the forest above Daranak Falls, reached in about
10–20 minutes
on foot past the Daranak entrance, across bridges, stairs, and streams. A chain of small stepped cascades and several pools, it is quieter and more natural than Daranak, making it a good add-on stop.

The Baroque-style San Ildefonso de Toledo Church, built in the Spanish era, is a designated national cultural treasure for its Rococo altar and wood-carved Stations of the Cross. It's right in the town center, easy to stop by on the way.

blocks.title: The giant Marian statue at Regina Rica

children.text: A retreat facility run by a religious sisterhood on a hill near Marcos Highway, with a giant statue of the Virgin Mary, gardens, and mountain views. Opening days and admission fees are set, so check before you visit.

The mountain road linking Antipolo to Tanay is lined with cafes and restaurants overlooking the Sierra Madre ridges and Laguna Lake. It's a good spot to rest and watch the sunset on your way back from the falls.

Around the Tanay public market, where you catch a tricycle to the falls, you'll find freshwater fish from Laguna Lake, mountain-grown fruit, and rice-cake snacks. Pick up picnic food and soak in the country-market atmosphere.

If you're traveling by public transport, a half-day itinerary combining just Daranak Falls and Tanay Church is more realistic. Regina Rica and the view cafes are spread apart, so a vehicle makes getting around much easier.
From Manila, follow Ortigas Avenue Extension through Teresa, Morong, and Baras to Tanay, or take Manila East Road past the towns along Laguna Lake. It takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours 30 minutes
, and it's about
15–20 minutes
from downtown Tanay to the falls entrance. There's a parking lot near the entrance.
By Grab, it's about
one way from eastern Metro Manila, but since it's hard to catch a ride back from Tanay, a round-trip charter is a better choice.
Near Star Mall (EDSA Central) on Shaw Boulevard in Mandaluyong, take a UV Express van or jeepney bound for Tanay. It takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
, for a fare of about
, and you get off near the Tanay market (public market).
You can also get off at LRT-2 Antipolo Station and switch to a bus or jeepney bound for Tanay/Pililla in front of the nearby SM Masinag.
From the tricycle stand in front of Tanay market, it's about
one way per vehicle to the falls. Tricycles for the return trip can be scarce near the falls, so it's better to negotiate a round trip or an hourly rate that includes waiting (about
including Batlag).
The dry season,
November–May
, is best, with clear water and good roads. The ideal time to swim is
March–May
, when midday temperatures climb to
and the cold falls water is especially welcome. That said, the pool fills with crowds during Holy Week and summer-break weekends, so aim for a weekday morning.
December–February
has fairly cold water, better suited to sightseeing and picnicking than swimming.
During the wet season,
June–October

, higher water volume makes the falls more dramatic, but after rain the water turns muddy and the current picks up. Entry is closed for safety during heavy rain or typhoon warnings, so check notices from the Tanay tourism office. Every year in the
third week of January
, a rodeo festival celebrating Tanay's ranching culture adds to the sights.

Most visitors come from Manila for the day, but staying overnight in Tanay lets you comfortably combine the trip with Mount Daraitan or Masungi Georeserve the next day. Downtown has simple lodges and inns (about
per night), and the uplands around Marcos Highway have a cluster of resorts and glamping sites with mountain views (about
per night), good for enjoying the cooler mountain air.

Around the falls entrance are small shops selling drinks, snacks, and instant noodles, but food options are limited, so, as Filipinos do, bringing rice and side dishes to eat at a hut is the most enjoyable option. Picking up whole roast pork lechon, grilled chicken, and fruit from Tanay market on the way makes for a great picnic. Restaurants in town serve Filipino home cooking like adobo, sinigang, and pancit for about
a meal, and in the evening, enjoy the mountain scenery at a Marcos Highway view restaurant over grilled pork inihaw or beef bone soup bulalo.
The falls are generally open
8 AM–5 PM
. Go right after opening for the clearest water and the best pick of huts.
It gets very crowded on weekends, public holidays, and Holy Week. Go on a weekday for a quieter visit.
The pool floor and rocks are slippery. Aqua shoes make things much more comfortable and safe.
Changing rooms and showers are basic, so bring a towel, a change of clothes, and a plastic bag.
Admission and hut rental are often cash only. Bring plenty of small bills.
Agreeing on a return time with your tricycle driver in advance saves a long wait at the falls.
Bring your phone and camera in a dry bag. Spray in front of the falls quickly wets lenses, so a lens cloth is handy too.
Two to three hours is enough for Daranak Falls alone. If you're spending a full day, add one of Batlag Falls, Masungi Georeserve, or Mount Daraitan to your plan.
Always carry your trash out or dispose of it in designated bins. Don't use soap or shampoo in the falls water.
Daranak Falls reopened on
March 2, 2026
after completing repair work. There are also spots for pitching a tent (about

), and in typhoons or heavy rain the city of Tanay suspends outdoor tourism such as swimming and canyon trekking altogether, so in the rainy season check the Tanay tourism office's Facebook notices before you set out.
The current is strong and the water deep right below the falls. Don't go under the falling water or jump off the rocks, and always put a life vest on children and watch them closely.
After heavy rain, the water can rise suddenly and turn murky. Get out of the water immediately if the color changes or staff direct an evacuation.
The falls water is very cold. Staying in too long can lower your body temperature, so dry off periodically.
On crowded days, keep a close eye on belongings left at your hut, and keep valuables in the car or on your person.
Swimming after drinking is very dangerous. Management rules sometimes restrict bringing in alcohol as well.
